title: Association calls for balanced compliance
full_text:
The SMSF Association has called for the ATO to take a balanced approach in its regulation of the sector while tackling genuine misconduct quickly when it is identified, and at the same time calling for definitive guidance on key matters.
The professional body made the calls in its submission to the Australian National Audit Office’s (ANAO) performance audit of the ATO’s regulation of SMSFs where it noted the review was timely given the last one was carried out in 2007 and since then the sector had grown substantially to more than $1 trillion in retirement savings.
“We recognise that the regulatory environment has become more complex and the ATO’s role has evolved from a largely educative model to a more active regulatory model,” the submission stated.
“For the ATO, the practical challenge is the identification and response to genuine misconduct without imposing unnecessary delay, uncertainty or administrative burden on compliant funds.
“We consider the audit should test whether the ATO’s administration is sufficiently risk-based, proportionate, transparent and timely, and whether its compliance tools distinguish serious or deliberate non-compliance from administrative failure, inadvertent error and issues that can be efficiently rectified.”
The association noted while the regulator had significant data, powers and compliance tools, that framework did not always make the distinction mentioned above and could lead to disproportionate consequences for low-risk conduct and slower responses to serious cases or recurring structural gaps.
SMSF Association chief Peter Burgess added: “We fully support a regulatory framework that is firm where it needs to be, practical in its administration, clear about the scope of the ATO’s role and supportive of trustees and professionals who are committed to doing the right thing.”
Burgess pointed to the operational consequences of a late SMSF annual return lodgement as an example of a low-risk, unintentional breach.
“Timely lodgement is essential, but a short delay can disrupt contributions and rollovers, creating additional work and uncertainty for members and employers well beyond the overdue return,” he said.
“We want proportionate responses and pragmatic resolutions that support compliance without imposing consequences beyond what the underlying risk warrants.”
The submission also called on the ANAO to review the ATO’s public advice and guidance framework, including its use of non-binding web content, the currency of SMSF-specific rulings and access to authoritative advice on Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Act issues.
“Clear, timely guidance is a frontline compliance tool. It helps prevent inadvertent breaches and allows enforcement resources to focus on genuine integrity risks,” Burgess added.
“Web content has an important role, but trustees and professionals also need durable, authoritative explanations of how the ATO applies the law, particularly where the consequences are significant.”
author: Jason Spits
